mstts:express-as.prosody: Let’s talk about something really important: Embracing Intersectionality—Understanding Overlapping Identities. When we’re raising feminist kids, it’s easy to focus on gender. But here’s the thing—gender isn’t the only piece of the puzzle. There’s race, class, ability, sexuality, religion... and all of these parts come together to shape who someone is and what they experience. That idea is called intersectionality. Imagine every child as a mosaic, with each little tile representing a piece of their identity. Intersectionality helps us see every child as unique, with their own combination of stories, strengths, and challenges. So, how do we teach kids about this? It all starts with curiosity and empathy. Instead of encouraging children to “not see differences,” we can invite them to notice and appreciate what makes people unique. Maybe you read books together that feature all kinds of characters. Or you take time to learn about different cultures, and chat about what’s happening in the world—in ways that make sense for their age. Here are a few ways you can really embrace intersectionality: First, listen to and validate what people from other backgrounds share about their lives. Next, try challenging stereotypes and assumptions—both in yourself and when you hear them from others. And encourage kids to speak up against injustice, even if it doesn’t affect them directly. Let’s say your child notices a classmate being treated unfairly because of their race or disability. That’s a powerful moment. You can help them learn how to show support—maybe by standing up against exclusion, inviting the classmate to join in, or just being a kind friend who listens. Intersectionality also means looking at your own advantages and asking, “How can I use what I have to help others?” When caregivers model this—like by talking about their own privileges and taking real action to challenge inequality—kids pick up on it. When you help children see the world through an intersectional lens, you’re giving them the tools to be more just, more compassionate, and more inclusive. That’s how we raise thoughtful leaders and true allies for a diverse world.
